millennials-first-homes.headline: Millennials finding it easier to buy first homes as market turns
millennials-first-homes.body_md:
For most of the past two decades, the story of millennial homeownership in Britain has been a one-way ratchet: prices up, deposits up, the age of the first-time buyer creeping later with each cohort. New figures suggest that ratchet may finally be loosening.

The headline number comes from a comparison of birth cohorts. Britons born in 1961-65 had a 47% chance of owning a home by age 28. Those born in 1991-95 — the youngest millennials — managed just 27% by the same age. That gap is the definitive story of a generation locked out. But the more recent trend line has turned: house prices, which stood at roughly nine times average income in 2021, have eased to about 7.6 times income this year, according to data cited in BBC reporting this week. It's not a return to the affordability of the 1990s. It is, for the first time in a long while, movement in the right direction.

## What's actually changed

Three things have shifted since the post-pandemic peak, and none of them is dramatic on its own.

First, wages have outpaced house prices for several consecutive years, narrowing the price-to-earnings ratio mechanically rather than through any single policy intervention. Second, mortgage products have adapted: some lenders now offer 5% deposit mortgages, down from the 10-15% that became standard after the 2008 crisis, and terms have stretched to 40 years from the traditional 25-30, lowering monthly payments even as headline rates stay elevated. Two-year fixed mortgage rates were averaging 5.63% and five-year fixes 5.66% in early August, with markets pricing in further Bank of England cuts from the current 3.75% base rate at the September and November meetings.

Third, and less visibly, the burden has fallen. Mortgage payments for a typical first-time buyer now consume about 32% of take-home pay, close to the long-run average of 30% and well below the 45% peak reached in 2007. Private renters, by contrast, are still handing over roughly 32% of income in rent — meaning buying and renting now cost, in relative terms, about the same. That parity is new, and it changes the calculation for anyone who has been sitting on the fence.

![Terraced housing in Loughborough, England](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e7/Street_of_terraced_housing.jpg)

## The deposit still bites

None of this erases the deposit problem, which remains the single biggest barrier cited by prospective buyers. A 10% deposit on a typical first-time buyer property costs £44,800 in London, £32,800 in the outer metropolitan ring, and £13,100 in the north of England — a near fourfold regional spread that means the "easier" story is really a regional and income-dependent one. Over a third of first-time buyers now receive help from family, whether as a gift, a loan or an inheritance, according to lender data — a dependency that widens the gap between buyers with property-owning parents and those without.

Supply remains the binding constraint behind all of it. England needs roughly 300,000 new homes a year to keep pace with demand, by the government's own estimate; only around 208,000 were completed last year. Building costs have risen 50% since 2015 against 35% general inflation, partly a legacy of the energy price shock that followed Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which pushed construction energy costs up 15% in a single year. A home that cost £150,000 to build in 2015 costs roughly £230,000 today, with a further 15% rise projected over five years — a cost base that limits how far builders can pass on price relief even as the government pushes planning reform and looser green-belt rules to unlock sites.

## Why markets should care

A millennial cohort re-entering the housing market matters beyond the individual balance sheets involved. Housing transactions pull through demand for furniture, white goods, renovation and removals spending — a multiplier effect that shows up in retail and construction earnings before it shows up in GDP data. A sustained pickup in first-time buyer activity would also support materials and housebuilder equities, which have spent much of the past three years pricing in a structurally weak demand backdrop.

The interest-rate read-through cuts the other way, and matters more to the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee. Improving affordability driven partly by wage growth outpacing prices is not obviously disinflationary — it reflects income gains that could keep services inflation stickier than the Bank would like, one reason six of nine MPC members opted to hold rates at 3.75% in July against three dissenters pushing for a rise. Whether the September 17 meeting delivers the cut markets are pricing will hinge on whether that private-sector wage growth, running at its weakest pace since 2020 by some measures, continues to cool.

The honest reading of the data is that this is a partial, uneven recovery rather than a regime shift: the youngest millennials are still buying homes at little more than half the rate their parents' generation did at the same age. But after years in which every affordability metric moved the wrong way, a price-to-earnings ratio falling from nine to 7.6 and a rent-versus-mortgage gap closing to near-parity are real, measurable improvements. The next data points worth watching are the Bank's September rate decision and the autumn house-price indices from Halifax and Nationwide, which will show whether this year's affordability gains survive contact with the traditionally busier back-to-school buying season.
millennials-first-homes.in_one_sentence: UK house prices have fallen from nine times to 7.6 times average income since 2021, giving millennials their best affordability window in years — though deposits and housing supply remain binding constraints.

airbus-rto-reversal.headline: Airbus backs down on return-to-office mandate after union strikes
airbus-rto-reversal.body_md:
For six weeks this summer, the sound of an aerospace giant absorbing a labour defeat was mostly quiet — a three-hour stoppage here, a march outside a Toulouse office there, ballots being counted in Getafe and Filton. But by the third week of August, Airbus's management had done something European unions had been trying to get a major multinational to do for years: reverse a return-to-office mandate under direct strike pressure, in public, without much room to dress it up as anything else.

![Airbus's Wings Campus headquarters near Toulouse-Blagnac, France](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/Toulouse_Si%C3%A8ge_Airbus.jpg)

## The mandate, and the memo that triggered it

The dispute traces back to a memo chief executive Guillaume Faury sent staff in June, telling white-collar employees they would need to be in the office four days a week by September, up from three. Faury framed it as a matter of institutional survival rather than nostalgia for pre-pandemic habits: with a quarter to a third of Airbus's workforce hired within the last three years — the product of heavy post-Covid attrition across aerospace — he argued the company was losing the informal, hallway transfer of engineering knowledge that new hires need and that video calls don't replicate. "I count on all of you to support this," he told employees.

Support was not forthcoming, at least not in Spain. SIPA, an independent union representing aeronautical professionals, called a strike on July 1 over the policy, and was quickly joined by UGT and CGT. Comisiones Obreras, the largest union among Airbus's roughly 14,000 Spanish employees, held back from formal action but let it be known it was prepared to call an indefinite strike of its own after September 7 if the mandate went ahead unchanged. Spanish unions estimate that around 40% of the workforce there took part in some form of walkout over the summer — grievances that, notably, went beyond teleworking to include transport allowances, paid leave and pay. Sympathy protests, smaller and more sporadic, appeared outside Airbus sites in France and Britain.

## Retreat, calibrated but real

Airbus was careful about how it climbed down. Rather than rescinding the four-day policy outright, managers were told this week to let existing arrangements stand: employees can keep working from home roughly two days a week on average, and the harder one-day ceiling that was due to bite in September has been shelved indefinitely rather than formally scrapped. A company spokesperson insisted the underlying goal hadn't changed — "our objective remains the same: we aim for increased on-site presence to ensure better collective efficiency, knowledge transfer and faster decision-making" — while conceding that getting there "requires listening to our people" and implementing the shift "more gradually."

![Guillaume Faury, Airbus's chief executive, pictured at the European Commission in Brussels in 2023](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ad/Guillaume_Faury_-_2023_%28cropped%29.jpg)

That is corporate language for a concession, and unions treated it as one. Crucially, the disruption never touched aircraft assembly lines — the strikes were confined to white-collar support functions, meaning Airbus's delivery schedule, already under close market scrutiny after years of supply-chain strain, was never seriously at risk. Management could plausibly have ridden out the unrest on production grounds alone. That it chose not to suggests the reputational and recruitment costs of a prolonged standoff — in a labour market where aerospace employers are already struggling to attract engineers who prioritise flexibility — weighed more heavily than the strikes' direct economic bite.

## Why the retreat travels beyond Toulouse

Return-to-office pushes have largely gone the employer's way since 2023: Amazon, JPMorgan and others have tightened attendance rules with limited organised pushback, in part because remote-work advocates in tech and finance are rarely unionised at scale. Airbus is different — a heavily unionised, works-council-governed European employer where a coordinated strike threat carries real institutional weight, and where the fight over hybrid work fused with older, harder-edged disputes over pay and conditions. That combination is what forced a public retreat rather than a quiet compromise.

The episode is likely to be read closely by works councils and union federations elsewhere in European manufacturing and aviation, sectors where hybrid-work fights have simmered without producing a comparable capitulation. It also lands as a data point for a broader argument gaining currency among labour economists: that a tight market for skilled engineering and technical talent, combined with organised representation, gives workers leverage over scheduling questions that goes well beyond wages. For Airbus shareholders, the immediate financial exposure is negligible — this was a white-collar dispute that never touched the factory floor. The more durable cost is strategic: Faury's knowledge-transfer rationale for in-person work remains unresolved, and the company has bought time rather than settled the underlying question of how it retools its workforce.

CCOO's threatened indefinite strike, contingent on developments after September 7, remains the next flashpoint to watch — a test of whether Spain's largest union sees the current concession as sufficient or merely as proof that pressure works.

albania-deportations-legal-challenge.headline: Home Office could be blocked from deporting trafficking victims to Albania
albania-deportations-legal-challenge.body_md:
A ruling from a panel of three senior judges in London this month has opened a fresh legal front against one of the Home Office's most heavily relied-upon deportation routes — and could force ministers to rethink how they treat some of the asylum system's most vulnerable claimants.

The Upper Tribunal's Immigration and Asylum Chamber found that a 21-year-old Albanian man, trafficked into cannabis cultivation as a teenager, remained at "real risk" of being retrafficked if returned to Albania — despite five years having passed since he first fled his exploiters. In doing so, the judges issued new country guidance that the Home Office must now factor into every future decision on whether to remove male trafficking victims to Albania. It is a narrow ruling on paper. In practice, lawyers say it strikes at the foundation of a returns strategy the government has leaned on for four years to bring down Channel crossing numbers and clear the asylum backlog.

![Royal Courts of Justice, London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7c/Royal_Courts_of_Justice_2019.jpg)

## A well-worn deportation pipeline hits a wall

Albania occupies a peculiar place in Britain's asylum system. It is not a country in conflict, and the Home Office has long treated it as broadly "safe" — a classification that underpins a 2022 returns agreement, struck after more than 10,000 Albanians arrived by small boat that year alone, roughly a quarter of all Channel crossings. Rishi Sunak's government responded with a dedicated Home Office unit to fast-track Albanian claims and a bilateral deal with Tirana to put failed applicants on removal flights. It worked, in volume terms: Albanians have been the single largest nationality among enforced removals from the UK for five consecutive years, with 2,247 deported in the twelve months to the end of March, roughly a quarter of all enforced returns.

But the same period saw a quieter, parallel trend. Referrals of Albanian males into the UK's National Referral Mechanism for suspected trafficking victims overtook referrals of Albanian women for the first time — 4,107 men and boys flagged in 2022, against 502 women, with the pattern holding in 2023 at 3,463 to 588. Most were trafficked not for sex but for labour, typically cultivating cannabis in rented houses under the control of organised crime networks that operate on both sides of the Channel. The government's "safe country" framing and the reality facing this specific population — recognised trafficking victims, disproportionately young men — have been on a collision course for some time. This ruling is where they met.

## What the tribunal found

The case centred on a young man first exploited by an Albanian gang while visiting Belgium with his father at 16, then trafficked onward to the UK and forced into cannabis cultivation. He escaped, was formally recognised by the Home Office as a trafficking victim through the National Referral Mechanism, and was subsequently denied asylum on the basis that Albania was safe for him to return to.

The tribunal disagreed. Its judgment, examined in detail by three senior judges, concluded that although Albania has made genuine progress against corruption, it remains "widespread," that there are no dedicated shelters for adult male trafficking victims anywhere in the country, and that the risk of retrafficking for men in this position is significant — regardless of how much time has elapsed since the original exploitation. Because it was issued as country guidance rather than a one-off decision, the finding binds future tribunals and obliges Home Office caseworkers to grapple with it directly, rather than treating each Albanian male trafficking case in isolation.

> "[This] measured judgment reflects the significant and detailed evidence... about the organised criminal networks that target and control boys and young men."

That assessment came from Esme Madill, a solicitor at Islington Law Centre who represented the claimant and has spent years working on Albanian trafficking cases through the Breaking the Chains project, a joint initiative with the Shpresa Programme focused on young Albanian asylum seekers. Home Office sources indicated they were weighing whether to appeal.

## The stakes for enforcement policy

![Tirana, Albania](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a0/TiranaPhotoCollage.jpg)

The political backdrop makes the timing awkward for the government. The headline asylum numbers have been moving in the direction ministers want: the initial-decision backlog stood at 35,744 applications at the end of March, down 58% since June 2024 and the lowest level since 2020. Albanian removals have been central to that progress, both as a volume driver and as a deterrent signal to prospective Channel crossers. A country-guidance ruling that requires individualised scrutiny of trafficking history before any Albanian male can be removed complicates that machinery considerably — it does not halt removals outright, but it raises the evidential bar for each one and hands defence lawyers a binding precedent to invoke.

It also lands as the broader system strains elsewhere: the appeals backlog, distinct from the initial-decision queue the government has been trumpeting, nearly doubled last year to a record 80,000 cases. Every case where a trafficking claim now requires fresh consideration under this guidance is a case that risks feeding directly into that queue rather than clearing out the front door.

The deeper tension the ruling exposes is not really about Albania specifically. It is about whether a general "safe country" designation can survive contact with a well-evidenced, population-specific protection claim — in this instance, that organised crime in Albania targets and re-targets trafficked men in a way generic country assessments miss. Courts have shown, in this judgment, that they will not defer to enforcement targets when the evidence points the other way.

## What happens next

The immediate question is whether the Home Office appeals the ruling to the Court of Appeal, a decision expected in the coming weeks. Either way, caseworkers must now apply the new country guidance to pending and future Albanian male trafficking claims, which is likely to slow individual case processing even as the government continues to publicise backlog reductions elsewhere. Immigration lawyers expect a wave of fresh challenges from Albanian men already served with removal directions, testing how far the ruling's protection extends beyond the specific facts of this case.

baker-hughes-rig-count.headline: US rig count falls again as oil and gas drilling activity softens
baker-hughes-rig-count.body_md:
US drillers idled rigs again last week, extending a soft patch that has become the summer's quiet undertone in the oil patch. Baker Hughes' weekly count, released Friday, showed the total US rig count down five to 588 for the week ended August 21 — oil-directed rigs off three to 452, gas rigs down one to 127, and miscellaneous rigs down one to 9.

On its own, that is a small number in a slow-moving series. The count had actually risen five rigs the week before, to 593, its highest mark since March 2025, so last week's pullback erased almost exactly what the prior week added. Read across a month rather than a week, the trend is closer to flat-with-a-downward-lean than a rout: the total remains roughly 9% above where it stood a year ago, when the US was running around 539 rigs.

![A Marcellus Shale gas drilling rig tower](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7b/Marcellus_Shale_Gas_Drilling_Tower_1.jpg)

## Prices are up. Rigs mostly aren't.

What makes the flatness notable is the backdrop it's happening against. West Texas Intermediate has been trading near $84 a barrel this month, propped up by the standoff over Iran and repeated disruptions to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. In an earlier cycle, prices at that level would typically have pulled a wave of new rigs into the field. This time the response has been muted, and that gap between price and activity is the more useful story than the weekly rig tally itself.

The explanation operators and analysts point to is capital discipline that has outlasted the price spike. Since the investor revolt against shale's growth-at-all-costs era, producers have leaned on longer laterals and more efficient completions to keep output climbing even as rig counts stay well below their 2022 peak — Lower 48 crude production has been running near record highs, above 13.7 million barrels a day, on fewer rigs than a year ago. Wall Street has told management teams it wants free cash flow and buybacks, not a repeat of the drilling binges that wrecked returns the last time crude ran hot.

The basin-level detail from last week fits that pattern more than it contradicts it. The Permian and the Eagle Ford both added rigs even as the national total fell, while the gas-heavy Haynesville lost two and the Granite Wash lost one — a split that looks more like reshuffling toward the most productive oil acreage than a broad retreat from drilling.

None of this settles whether the softening is capital discipline holding firm or the first sign of demand-side hesitation creeping into investment plans. That distinction won't come from any single Friday print. It will come from whether the Permian keeps adding through the autumn even if headline prices soften, and from the next round of EIA production revisions, due in the Short-Term Energy Outlook next month, which will show whether output is still climbing on fewer rigs or beginning to plateau.

kryvyi-rih-strike.headline: Russian strike on Kryvyi Rih shopping centre kills at least 16
kryvyi-rih-strike.body_md:
Shortly after lunchtime on Friday, drones struck a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih, the industrial city in central Ukraine that happens to be President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown. As fire crews arrived to fight the blaze and pull survivors from the wreckage, a second wave of drones hit the same building roughly thirty minutes later. By Saturday morning the death toll stood at 16, with more than 130 people wounded — 23 of them children — and nine more, including two children, still unaccounted for beneath the rubble.

Ukrainian officials call the tactic a "double-tap" strike: hit a target, wait for rescuers to converge, then hit it again. Zelensky, who was blunt in his fury, called it "an absolute Russian atrocity" and said those responsible were "monsters." Asked what Ukraine would do next, his answer was terse. "We will definitely respond," he said, without elaborating on how.

![Volodymyr Zelensky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/Volodymyr_Zelensky_2022_official_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## A city that has been hit before

Kryvyi Rih is no stranger to this war. The city — Europe's longest, strung along more than 60 kilometres of former iron-ore workings — has absorbed repeated Russian strikes since 2022, including a missile attack on a residential building in April 2025 that killed civilians in a different incident from Friday's. What distinguishes this latest strike is less its scale than its symbolism and its method: a shopping centre, not a barracks or a power substation, hit twice in short succession during daylight hours, with emergency responders caught in the second wave.

Al Jazeera and the BBC, among others, reported the toll rising through Friday night as rescue crews worked the site with heavy equipment and dogs. The shopping and entertainment complex, known locally as Sunny Gallery, was reduced to a shell; residents described the second detonation as louder than the first, a detail consistent with the double-tap pattern Ukrainian officials have documented in strikes elsewhere in the country this year.

![Kryvyi Rih](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/Kryvyi_Rih_%28collage%29.jpg)

## The other half of the exchange

Ukraine's response, if Friday's rhetoric is any guide, is likely to look like what it has looked like for most of 2026: long-range drone strikes on Russian refining capacity, not a symmetrical hit on a civilian target. Overnight into Saturday, a fire broke out at the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia's Samara Oblast after a Ukrainian drone attack — one of the largest refineries in the Volga region, with roughly 8.8 million tonnes of annual capacity, and a repeat target after strikes in April, May and earlier in August. It is part of a methodical campaign: Ukraine has worked through the Russian refining system plant by plant this year, with Saratov, Kirishi and Norsi among the facilities that have lost capacity to repeated attacks.

![Fire at an oil refinery](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ec/Fire_at_the_Moscow_Oil_Refinery_on_June_18%2C_2026_%2820260618_132807%29.jpg)

The campaign is showing up in markets. Russian oil shipments from western ports fell to about 2.3 million barrels a day in the first half of August, some 15% below plan, largely because of disruptions at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk. Brent crude has been climbing in tandem, trading above $91 a barrel and on track for a second consecutive weekly gain, with analysts citing a rising geopolitical risk premium alongside separate tensions in the Middle East. Global diesel markets, which depend heavily on Russian refined exports, have felt the tightening most acutely.

## No exit from the cycle

What makes Friday's strike notable for anyone tracking risk rather than just the war itself is not its individual horror — Kryvyi Rih has suffered worse tolls before — but its place in a pattern that shows no sign of breaking. Russia keeps hitting Ukrainian population centres and, increasingly, targets that look designed to kill first responders. Ukraine keeps hitting Russian energy infrastructure, methodically and at increasing tempo. Neither side has given any public indication it sees an off-ramp, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv has faced a battlefield or diplomatic shock large enough to change the calculus.

For markets, the implication is less about any single event moving prices sharply than about a floor being built under the risk premium — energy traders now treat continued mutual escalation as the base case rather than a tail risk. The next data points worth watching are mundane by comparison to Friday's toll: whether Novorossiysk's export disruptions persist into September, whether Russia's refining losses show up in diesel cracks, and whether Zelensky's promised response takes the form of another refinery strike or something that raises the stakes further.

north-sea-licensing-row.headline: Labour accused of stalling on Jackdaw and Rosebank North Sea projects
north-sea-licensing-row.body_md:
Kemi Badenoch has a straightforward diagnosis of why two of the North Sea's largest undeveloped oil and gas fields are still waiting for a green light: the government doesn't really want to give them one.

"If this decision had been made earlier in the summer, we could have had gas from Jackdaw in people's homes by this winter, by Christmas," the Conservative leader said, accusing Labour of dragging its feet on approvals for the Jackdaw gas field and the Rosebank oil field. Their "heart's not really in it," she added — a jab less at process than at motive.

The timing is pointed. Public consultations on both projects have now closed — Jackdaw's just over a week ago, Rosebank's more recently — which normally would clear the way for a ministerial decision. Instead, officials have declined to set a deadline. "We've not put a particular deadline on it, but we have gone as fast as we can through every stage of this process," one government source said when asked whether a call would land in September.

## Two fields, two fates

Jackdaw, a Shell-operated gas field roughly 150 miles east of Aberdeen, was first approved back in 2022. Rosebank, west of Shetland and jointly owned by Equinor and Shell through the Adura venture, is the larger prize — up to 500 million barrels of oil, and the UK's biggest untapped field. Both had their consents quashed last year after a legal challenge succeeded in the courts, forcing the fresh consultation round that has just concluded.

Reporting in recent days suggests the government may be preparing to split the difference: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is said to be "minded to approve" Jackdaw, while Labour figures have privately signalled that Rosebank — facing fiercer climate objections — may be rejected. One option under discussion, according to reports, is delaying any announcement until public attention has moved past the summer's heatwave coverage, to blunt the political fallout either way.

The final sign-off rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has previously opposed new North Sea licensing but said in July she intended to be "pragmatic" on the question. That shift alone tells its own story about the pressure the government is under from unions and industry, who point to 3,500 construction jobs and 880 permanent roles the two fields could support.

## The pressure from the other side

Badenoch's complaint is not the only one landing on Burnham's desk. Ninety MPs and MSPs, organised by the environmental campaign group Uplift, wrote to the prime minister this month urging him to reject Rosebank outright, arguing the field would produce more than 250 million tonnes of CO2 over its lifetime — equivalent to roughly 70% of Britain's annual emissions — while adding barely 1% to the country's energy security, per an International Energy Agency assessment cited in the letter.

That squeeze — jobs and tax revenue on one side, emissions accounting and manifesto commitments on the other — is precisely why no deadline has been set. Every month of delay is itself a decision of sorts, just one nobody in government has to defend on the record.

![Kemi Badenoch](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d5/Official_portrait_of_Kemi_Badenoch_MP_crop_2%2C_2024.jpg)

For operators, the uncertainty carries a real cost: investment decisions, rig contracts and workforce planning don't wait comfortably on political timetables. Watch for Fahnbulleh's formal response to the consultations, expected in the coming weeks, and for whether Jackdaw and Rosebank are announced together or peeled apart — a split verdict would tell its own story about how Burnham is trying to have this both ways.

bessent-iran-sanctions.headline: Bessent touts 'toughest sanctions yet' on Iran as US futures gain
bessent-iran-sanctions.body_md:
US stock futures ticked higher on Friday after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington is preparing "the toughest sanctions in history" against Iran — a phrase that, this time, appears to have done more for the pre-market mood than for anyone's actual understanding of what comes next.

Dow futures rose 0.35%, the S&P 500 0.30%, the Nasdaq 100 0.46% and the small-cap Russell 2000 0.54%, clawing back part of Thursday's broader decline. Gold added 1.38% to around $4,581 an ounce and bitcoin jumped 9.4% to roughly $78,459 — moves more consistent with a market seeking havens and risk simultaneously than one confidently pricing a specific sanctions package. Crude, notably, did not follow the equity optimism: West Texas Intermediate slipped 0.86% to about $86.08 a barrel.

![Scott Bessent, official Treasury portrait](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/72/Scott_Bessent%2C_official_portrait_%282025%29.jpg)

## What Bessent actually said

Speaking as the US-Israel military campaign against Iran approaches its sixth month, Bessent described the coming measures as "the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world" and told international partners flatly: "You're either with us or against us." He said a fuller briefing would follow at a Monday press conference — meaning Friday's rally traded on a promise of details, not the details themselves.

Pressed on whether China, which buys more than 80% of Iran's seaborne oil exports according to analytics firm Kpler, would be targeted directly, Bessent demurred, saying sensitive discussions happen "in private." He argued that China's reliance on Gulf energy — roughly half its supply — should be incentive enough to cooperate. That is a bet on Beijing's self-interest, not a sanctions designation, and markets have no way to price the difference.

The concrete step announced alongside the rhetoric was narrower: new designations against ten individuals tied to Hezbollah's financial network, including a Turkish businessman accused of facilitating transactions. Sanctions specialists have long noted that Iran's economy has already absorbed successive rounds of similar measures over more than a decade, which is part of why skepticism persists about whether another round — however loudly described — meaningfully changes Tehran's calculus.

## A pattern of "toughest yet"

Friday's line was not the first time Bessent has reached for superlatives. Treasury has previously touted sanctions on an Iran-linked maritime network and warned of consequences for any country offering Tehran an economic "lifeline," while President Trump has separately promised the "MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY." Each iteration has moved futures modestly on the day; none has yet been followed by a package whose scope was clear enough for energy or shipping desks to model with confidence.

The credibility gap showed up just a day earlier. Oil spiked sharply on Thursday — Brent crude climbed 2.4% to $93.78 a barrel and WTI 2.7% to $86.64 — and Bessent told reporters he didn't "really understand" why. Representative Ro Khanna's retort on social media was blunt: "I understand why, Scott. Your boss started a dumb war with no plan, and Americans are paying for it." Iran has restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, the channel for roughly a fifth of global oil and LNG flows, since the conflict began on February 28 — a fact that makes a Treasury official professing confusion over an oil spike a notable admission, whatever the political framing around it.

## Why the rally may not hold information

For traders, the distinction matters: a genuine escalation in enforcement — secondary sanctions on Chinese refiners, a crackdown on the shadow tanker fleet, restrictions reaching beyond Hezbollah's financing network — would be a real catalyst for energy and shipping exposure. A restatement of resolve, delivered days after the sanctions official in question could not explain the previous day's oil move, reads more as an attempt to steady sentiment ahead of the weekend than as new information the market can act on.

Monday's press conference is the actual data point to watch. Until Treasury publishes designations, timelines and enforcement mechanisms — and until it clarifies whether China faces direct exposure — Friday's futures gain is best read as a bet on tone, not on substance.

china-hk-tech-rally.headline: China and Hong Kong stocks extend gains as Asian tech rally continues
china-hk-tech-rally.body_md:
China's large-cap CSI 300 edged up 0.57% to close near 4,619 on Friday, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 1.2%, or 310 points, to 26,009 — capping a week in which the city's benchmark rose roughly 3% and snapped a two-week losing streak. The Hang Seng Tech Index climbed 1.4% to 4,766. Turnover in Hong Kong ran to HK$257.28 billion, a sign the move was carried on real volume rather than thin holiday trade.

The pattern underneath the headline number is the more interesting part. Both indices were recovering, not simply advancing: the CSI 300 had tumbled 3% on Wednesday in a broad tech selloff, and Hong Kong had been almost flat the same day. What changed was Wall Street. A rout early Wednesday — the Dow was down as much as 700 points at one point after investors judged the US Treasury's newly expanded long-bond buyback plan insufficient to hold yields down — reversed by the close, helped along by a bond rally and a jolt from biotech, where Moderna surged as much as 160% and Merck jumped 12% on cancer-treatment data. That reversal snapped Wall Street's own three-day losing streak and gave Asia something to chase into Thursday: China's vaccine and biotech index shot up 10%, Hong Kong's innovative-drug gauge rose more than 8%, and tech shares clawed back some of Wednesday's losses.

## The yield story is messier than it looks

The tidy version of this rally is "stocks up because yields eased." The data only half supports it. The relief in Treasuries that lifted Wednesday's close had faded by Thursday, when the Nasdaq and S&P 500 slipped as the bond rally unwound, and yields resumed climbing into Friday — the 10-year rose another 3 basis points to 4.734%, the 30-year to 5.273%. Yet US equities kept rallying regardless: the Dow gained 517.80 points (0.98%) to 53,277.01 on Friday, the S&P 500 rose 0.43% to 7,674.37, and the Nasdaq added 0.43% to 26,180.45. Asia's tech names moved in step with that risk appetite rather than with the yield curve itself — evidence for the read that regional markets are pricing US policy direction, and shrugging off the day-to-day bond wobbles that would normally accompany it.

## Chips found their own reason to rally

Not everything traces back to Washington. South Korea's Kospi rose 0.88% to 6,912.95 on Friday on the back of Samsung Electronics, up 3.87% to 281,500 won, and SK Hynix, up 2.31% to 1.73 million won, both lifted by reports of a shareholder-return package that could reach 110 trillion won. "A large-scale share buyback and cancellation announced by SK Hynix, along with growing expectations for stronger shareholder returns from Samsung Electronics, provided upward momentum for chip stocks and the broader local market," said Lee Kyoung-min at Daishin Securities. Notably, Korean chip stocks rose even as US Treasury yields resumed their climb the same day — a reminder that not every gain in the region is a rates trade.

The cleaner test comes in less than a week. Kevin Warsh delivers his first keynote as Fed chair at Jackson Hole on August 28, nineteen days ahead of the September 16-17 FOMC meeting — the same meeting at which three regional Fed presidents dissented in favour of a hike at the last gathering. If Asia's tech rally really is a leveraged bet on US rate cuts, Warsh's tone next week is where that bet gets marked to market.

google-hassabis-chairman.headline: Google consolidates AI leadership as Hassabis steps back to chairman role
google-hassabis-chairman.body_md:
Google spent the past decade selling Demis Hassabis as the embodiment of its AI ambitions — the DeepMind co-founder and Nobel laureate who beat cancer's protein-folding problem and, along the way, built the lab meant to get the company to artificial general intelligence first. This month, Google moved him out of the job that runs that lab day to day.

Hassabis is now chairman of Google DeepMind and chief scientist of parent company Alphabet, a shift confirmed in early August. Operational control of the roughly 8,000-person division — the Gemini models, the research agenda, the shipping deadlines — passes to Koray Kavukcuoglu, DeepMind's chief technology officer, who becomes senior vice president and reports directly to Alphabet chief executive Sundar Pichai. Hassabis keeps a foot in the building, chairing DeepMind, setting long-range AGI strategy, and continuing to run Alphabet's drug-discovery offshoot Isomorphic Labs. But the executive who built DeepMind into Google's flagship AI lab no longer owns its delivery.

![Demis Hassabis at the 2024 Nobel Prize ceremony in Stockholm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ab/Demis_Hassabis%2C_2024_Nobel_Prize_Laureate_in_Chemistry_6.jpg)

## Why now

The reshuffle follows a run of bad news that Google mostly avoided saying out loud. Gemini 3.5 Pro, its next flagship model, has now missed three release windows — June, mid-July, and beyond — while rivals kept shipping. Artificial Analysis, which benchmarks model performance, has Google's strongest publicly available model trailing offerings from Anthropic, OpenAI, several Chinese labs, xAI and Meta on intelligence scores. Engineers who spoke to Fortune pointed to a specific miss: the company underweighted coding capability just as coding became the metric enterprise customers actually care about.

The personnel bleed has been just as pointed. In June, AlphaFold co-inventor John Jumper left for Anthropic, taking colleagues Jonas Adler and Alexander Pritzel with him. Then, in the same week as the leadership reshuffle, Jeff Dean — a 27-year Google veteran and DeepMind's chief scientist — announced he was leaving alongside Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le to start an independent public-benefit corporation called Discovery Loop, aimed at automating scientific research. Google is, notably, a founding investor and cloud partner in the new venture — an unusually amicable way to lose your chief scientist, and a sign the split was managed rather than acrimonious.

## London loses ground

The less-discussed part of the reorganization is geographic. DeepMind was built and run out of London — Hassabis is British, and the lab retained a distinct identity even after its 2023 merger with Google Brain. That identity is now eroding. Kavukcuoglu relocated from London to Mountain View over the past year to take on the sprawling research-and-operations brief he now formally holds, and Sebastian Borgeaud, who leads a key AI coding effort, made the same move to California.

Engineers described the pattern to Forbes as a slow transfer of authority westward, with one calling it the "America-fication" of DeepMind — a shift, they said, from a research culture toward one where, in their words, "it's the loudest person in the room." Others cited asymmetric access to projects (Mountain View could see London's work; the reverse wasn't true) and open competition for computing resources between the two sites. A former researcher summed it up as an environment where "things are quite politicized based on who you report to."

![Google's former DeepMind office building at 6 Pancras Square, London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/45/Google-Deep_Mind_headquarters_in_London%2C_6_Pancras_Square.jpg)

The symbolism cuts both ways. Google is simultaneously investing in London — DeepMind and other Google teams are due to move this year into Platform 37, a new King's Cross building named for AlphaGo's famous "Move 37," designed by Thomas Heatherwick. But real decision-making authority over coding and product timelines is now sitting in California, and the people who used to hold it in London have either relocated or left the company.

## The commercialization problem

Strip away the individual moves and the pattern reads clearly: Google is separating scientific ambition from product execution, and betting that clearer lines of accountability fix a speed problem money alone hasn't. Hassabis was, by every account, an outstanding recruiter of research talent and a credible public face for "AI done safely." What DeepMind has struggled to do is ship a frontier model on schedule while OpenAI and Anthropic iterate faster and, increasingly, poach the researchers who'd otherwise close that gap. Putting one person — Kavukcuoglu — in sole charge of Gemini, research and product removes an ambiguity that reportedly cost DeepMind time internally, even if it does nothing by itself to close the technical distance to GPT-5-class or Claude-class models.

For anyone pricing Alphabet's AI position, the read is that the company has diagnosed its problem as organizational rather than purely technical — and organizational fixes are faster to execute than research breakthroughs, but they're also easier to get credit for without actually closing the gap. The next real test isn't a press release; it's whether Gemini 3.5 Pro ships on Kavukcuoglu's watch, and how it scores against Anthropic and OpenAI's models when it does. Alphabet reports third-quarter earnings in late October, by which point the market will want to know whether the new command structure produced a shipped model or just a cleaner org chart.

> "Things are quite politicized based on who you report to." — a former Google DeepMind researcher, on the London–Mountain View divide, quoted by Fortune

israel-west-bank-settlement.headline: Israel re-establishes closed West Bank settlement, defying international protest
israel-west-bank-settlement.body_md:
Two decades after Israeli bulldozers flattened it, the settlement of Ganim is standing again. On August 13, families began moving into around two dozen prefabricated homes on the hillside near Jenin in the northern West Bank — the site Israel evacuated in 2005 under Ariel Sharon's disengagement plan, alongside Gaza's Jewish settlements. It is the third of four settlements dismantled that year to be rebuilt this year alone, after Homesh in March and Sa-Nur in April.

![Israeli settlement construction in the West Bank](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8f/Illegal_israeli_settlements_southwestern_of_refugee_camp_Dheisheh%2C_Westbank%2C_Palestine.jpg)

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who doubles as the cabinet minister overseeing settlement policy, called the reopening the erasure of a "disgrace," referring to the 2005 pullout. Defence Minister Israel Katz was blunter: "Here, this is the Land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever." Yossi Dagan, who heads the regional settler council, declared "the era of evacuations is over." Palestinian stores near the site were demolished and access roads to neighbouring villages restricted ahead of the move-in, according to reporting from the ground.

## A pattern, not an incident

Ganim's reopening did not happen in isolation. A week later, Israel opened bidding for the E1 project — roughly 3,400 housing units on land between East Jerusalem and Ma'ale Adumim that would, if built, sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. Smotrich called E1 a plan that "practically erases the two-state delusion." UN Secretary-General António Guterres described it as an "existential threat" to a contiguous Palestinian state.

The response from Western governments was immediate and unusually broad. On 20-21 August, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada, Norway, Australia, New Zealand, Sweden, Belgium, Spain, Austria and Greece issued a joint statement branding the E1 tenders "unacceptable" and warning that "international law is clear that Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal." It went further than past statements, urging companies not to bid on the tenders and warning of "legal and reputational consequences" for firms that did. The same governments had already, in May, signed a separate statement over what they called "unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians" in the West Bank.

## Protest without cost

What stands out is less the criticism than the absence, so far, of anything behind it. Britain, Canada and Australia have condemned settlement expansion and demolitions repeatedly this year — over E1, over settler violence, over Israel's refusal to investigate the killing of aid workers in Gaza — without imposing sanctions, trade restrictions or arms measures tied specifically to West Bank policy. The corporate warning attached to the E1 statement is the sharpest tool used yet, and it relies on companies self-policing reputational risk rather than any government enforcement mechanism.

That gap is the story here for now: three settlements rebuilt, a fourth-largest settlement project advancing, and a coalition of Western governments whose criticism has grown louder each time without translating into material pressure. For markets, that is precisely why the episode has registered as noise rather than signal — oil prices and Israeli equities have shown little reaction to a dispute that remains, for now, rhetorical.

The next test is whether words turn into action. Israel's Higher Planning Committee is expected to advance further E1 construction approvals in the coming weeks, and the fourth evacuated settlement, Kadim, remains a likely candidate for reopening. Whether any signatory to the August statement follows through with concrete measures — rather than another joint letter — will determine whether this remains background noise in a two-decade-old conflict or becomes something markets need to start pricing.

tiktok-child-privacy-settlement.headline: TikTok to pay $400m in one of largest US child-privacy settlements
tiktok-child-privacy-settlement.body_md:
TikTok and its parent company ByteDance have agreed to pay $400 million to settle a US Justice Department lawsuit accusing the platform of harvesting children's personal data without parental consent — one of the largest recoveries the government has ever secured under federal child-privacy law.

![TikTok app icon on a smartphone screen](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/20/TikTok_app.jpg)

The settlement, announced Friday, closes a case the DOJ filed in 2024 alleging TikTok violated the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) by letting millions of under-13 users onto the platform and collecting their data anyway — despite, prosecutors said, having actual knowledge many of those accounts belonged to children. The suit also claimed TikTok kept that data for targeted advertising and altered its registration flow in ways that made it harder to catch underage sign-ups.

## The math behind $400 million

The payment breaks into two pieces. TikTok will hand over $300 million immediately. The remaining $100 million is tied to a separate, older matter: it's the price of vacating a 2019 consent order the Federal Trade Commission imposed on Musical.ly, the lip-syncing app ByteDance bought and folded into TikTok. That 2019 case ended with a $5.7 million fine — at the time the largest COPPA penalty on record. The new settlement is more than 70 times that figure, a gap that says less about inflation and more about how far the DOJ believes the underlying violations reached once TikTok had scaled to over a billion users.

Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward Jr. framed the outcome bluntly: "This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents." He added that the department's priority is "ensuring that children are protected online and that companies entrusted with their personal information meet their legal obligations." TikTok did not admit wrongdoing as part of the deal — standard practice in settlements of this size, and a reminder that the $400 million buys the company an exit from litigation, not a verdict.

## What TikTok has to change

Beyond the money, the settlement requires TikTok to strengthen age-verification controls, add new safeguards specifically for younger users, and give parents more direct oversight of their children's accounts and data. Those terms echo what regulators have demanded of other platforms in past COPPA cases — the mechanism is not novel — but the scale of enforcement against a company TikTok's size is.

The timing adds an edge to the story. Days before the settlement was announced, reports surfaced that TikTok had knowingly switched off algorithmic safety guardrails for roughly 10% of US users as part of an internal experiment, drawing bipartisan criticism in Washington. That disclosure sits awkwardly next to a company simultaneously agreeing to tighter child-safety commitments, and it suggests the DOJ's oversight of TikTok's practices is unlikely to end with this check.

## The read for the rest of the sector

What makes this settlement worth watching beyond TikTok itself is the precedent it sets for cost. Every major platform with a large teenage and pre-teen user base — YouTube, Instagram, Snapchat — operates under the same COPPA framework and the same basic exposure: undisclosed data collection from users too young to legally consent to it. A $400 million number, arrived at through negotiation rather than trial, gives regulators a fresh reference point for what "substantial recovery" looks like the next time one of TikTok's rivals ends up in the DOJ's sights. For an industry that has treated child-privacy fines as a rounding error against ad revenue, this is the first one big enough to actually register on a balance sheet.

The next marker to watch is enforcement of the settlement's behavioral terms — how the DOJ verifies TikTok's new age-checks and parental controls actually work, not just that they exist on paper.

hsbc-tokenised-deposit.headline: HSBC completes first live cross-border interbank tokenised deposit transaction
hsbc-tokenised-deposit.body_md:
HSBC and Standard Chartered have moved money between each other using bank-issued digital tokens instead of the usual correspondent-banking plumbing — a small transaction with a large ambition behind it.

The two banks said on 19 August they had completed the first live cross-border interbank transfer using tokenised deposits, settled via Swift's blockchain-based shared ledger. Neither disclosed the amount or currency. What mattered, in their telling, was that it happened at all: two separate institutions, each running its own token system, moved value between them without falling back on the decades-old network of correspondent accounts that normally handles cross-border payments.

![HSBC's Canary Wharf headquarters in London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3d/HSBC_Building_London.jpg)

## How it actually worked

A tokenised deposit is simply a bank's own ledger entry — the money in a corporate account — represented as a digital token rather than a row in a database. HSBC has offered this through its Tokenised Deposit Service since May 2025, initially in Hong Kong and since expanded to the US, UK and several Asian currencies including the yuan, dollar, euro and Emirati dirham.

The innovation this month was interoperability. HSBC's token system and Standard Chartered's separate one don't talk to each other directly. Swift's ledger — live since July after nine months of development — sat in between, passing payment messages that let each bank record matching obligations on its own books. Those obligations were then netted and settled through existing payment rails, the same ones banks have used for years. Nothing radical changed under the hood; what changed is that it happened around the clock, in principle, rather than only during the overlapping business hours of two national payment systems.

> "Digital money issued by banks can be interoperable across institutions while maintaining regulatory oversight of the existing financial ecosystem," said Lewis Sun, HSBC's head of digital currencies.

Standard Chartered's Mark Willis, head of emerging payments, called tokenised deposits "a key pillar" of the bank's digital assets strategy for cross-border liquidity.

## The bigger picture

Seventeen banks across six continents — including Citi, BNP Paribas, UBS, ANZ and DBS — are lined up to pilot transactions on Swift's ledger. Separately, a group of large US banks including JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo is building its own tokenised deposit network through The Clearing House, targeting a 2027 launch. Two rival infrastructures, in other words, both racing toward the same idea: banks want to keep settlement inside the regulated banking system rather than cede it to public blockchains or crypto exchanges.

That's the quiet subtext. Stablecoins and crypto rails have spent several years arguing they can move money faster and cheaper than banks can. HSBC and Swift's answer is to borrow the plumbing — distributed ledgers, always-on settlement — while keeping the money itself inside conventional bank deposits, with all the deposit insurance, capital rules and compliance that implies. If it works at scale, it undercuts one of crypto's core pitches to institutional treasurers: that only public blockchains can offer genuinely continuous settlement.

It is, for now, one transaction of undisclosed size between two banks that already work together constantly. The test is whether it stays a curiosity or becomes routine plumbing — the next marker will be whether disclosed volumes on Swift's ledger start showing up, and whether other banks in the 17-strong pilot group follow HSBC and Standard Chartered's lead before The Clearing House's rival network arrives in 2027.

london-datacentre-net-zero.headline: Proposed London datacentre deemed 'incompatible' with net zero over 1m-tonne carbon footprint
london-datacentre-net-zero.body_md:
A single planning application in outer London has put a number on a question the government has spent months avoiding: can Britain build the datacentres its AI boom demands and still hit net zero?

The East Havering Data Centre Campus, a proposed £14.7bn complex on 218 hectares of green belt farmland near North Ockendon, would be one of the largest datacentres in Europe. According to planning documents filed by its developer, Digital Reef, it would also generate more than 1.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a year once fully operational — roughly the same as 27,000 return flights from London to New York. Over its projected 60-year lifespan, the total comes to more than 72 million tonnes.

![A data centre server hall, illustrative of the type of facility proposed for North Ockendon](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5d/BalticServers_data_center.jpg)

> "It's crop-producing farmland, in an age when we are threatened by security, it's the loss of wildlife habitats, and there's the pollution cost."

That's the North Ockendon Residents Association, one of several local groups objecting to the scheme. But the more striking admission comes from the developer itself. Digital Reef's own submission concedes the project "does not align with a science-based 1.5C compatible trajectory and achieving net zero by 2050." Few applicants volunteer that their flagship project contradicts the government's core climate law.

## The numbers behind the objection

The scale is what makes East Havering unusual. The site would house up to 340,000 square metres of data centre space and draw around 2.65 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity annually — comparable to the demand of more than a million UK households, according to planning documents reviewed by the Guardian. By 2038, the campus's operational emissions alone would consume nearly 20 times the entire carbon budget allocated to the London borough of Havering, and close to 1% of the UK's national carbon budget.

Digital Reef has offered £77.6m toward the borough's carbon offset fund as mitigation. Campaigners, including the group Foxglove, argue that offsetting cash is the wrong tool for a problem this size. "It's a big threat to the ability to decarbonise in the UK," said Foxglove's Donald Campbell, who wants operators required to build dedicated renewable generation rather than pay into a fund.

## Not an isolated case

East Havering is the largest single scheme by disclosed emissions, but it sits inside a much bigger pipeline. Roughly 50 to 60 of the 100-plus datacentres currently working through planning in the UK are destined for London, with Havering, Tower Hamlets, Newham and Brent identified as the boroughs under most pressure. London Assembly members have been told that every ten new datacentres built could add around 2.7 million tonnes of emissions — a proliferation that assembly members warn could undermine the mayor's own climate targets even before East Havering is decided.

At Westminster, the discomfort runs upward too. The Commons Environmental Audit Committee, chaired by Labour MP Toby Perkins, has pressed energy secretary Ed Miliband on whether datacentre growth was ever factored into the plan to reach net zero. Miliband's written reply called the climate impact of the datacentre boom "inherently uncertain" — an answer that satisfied few of the MPs who asked the question.

## What happens next

Digital Reef is pursuing the scheme through a Local Development Order, a route that grants planning permission for a defined category of development while still requiring public consultation. An initial consultation closed in April; a revised proposal is expected before Havering council in autumn 2026, with a further consultation period to follow. The developer has also floated the possibility of applying for status as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project, which would shift the final decision away from the local council entirely and toward central government.

That procedural fork matters as much as the emissions figures. If ministers end up deciding East Havering's fate directly, the case becomes a test of whether the government will hold a project to its own net-zero commitments when the alternative is turning away £14.7bn in investment and the AI infrastructure capacity that comes with it. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has said datacentre emissions are already factored into its climate modelling and that its next carbon budget, covering the period to the 2040s, is due by the end of 2026 — the point at which this tension either gets resolved on paper or simply deferred again.

fda-approves-zenbexus.headline: FDA approves Bristol Myers Squibb's Zenbexus for multiple myeloma
fda-approves-zenbexus.body_md:
The FDA has approved Bristol Myers Squibb's Zenbexus, a new drug for adults with multiple myeloma who have relapsed after at least one prior round of treatment. It is a small approval in the sense that the patient population is narrow — this is not a first-line therapy — but it is a large one in the sense that Zenbexus is the first of an entirely new drug class, called CELMoDs, to reach the market for this cancer.

That distinction matters more than it might sound. Zenbexus, known chemically as iberdomide, is approved for use alongside two existing drugs — Johnson & Johnson's Darzalex (daratumumab) and the steroid dexamethasone — in patients who have already tried a proteasome inhibitor and an immunomodulatory drug, common building blocks of frontline myeloma regimens. The FDA granted the approval on August 13, based on results from the Phase 3 EXCALIBER-RRMM trial, in which 41% of patients on the Zenbexus combination reached a minimal-residual-disease-negative complete response, versus 21% on the comparator regimen — a statistically significant gap (p<0.0001), according to BMS's filing[^1].

![Bristol Myers Squibb's Princeton, New Jersey campus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0a/Bristol-Myers_Squibb_building_at_100_Nassau_Park_Boulevard_2010.jpg)

## A new mechanism, and a new yardstick

CELMoD stands for cereblon E3 ligase modulator — drugs that hijack a cell's own protein-disposal machinery to degrade proteins tumor cells depend on. It is a lineal descendant of the older "IMiD" class that includes BMS's own Revlimid, but engineered to bind cereblon more tightly and drive a broader set of proteins to destruction. Cristian Massacesi, BMS's chief medical officer, called it the arrival of "a new treatment class," adding that the approval "opens venues for many more potential combinations"[^2].

The approval is also notable on regulatory grounds: it is the first new multiple myeloma drug cleared using minimal residual disease — a blood test sensitive enough to detect a handful of cancer cells among a million healthy ones — as the primary evidence of benefit, rather than the traditional yardstick of progression-free survival. That is faster for patients and companies alike, but it comes with a catch: like other accelerated approvals, Zenbexus's continued marketing is contingent on BMS confirming real clinical benefit — meaning it actually helps patients live longer or better — in follow-up trials[^1].

## Why BMS needed this

The approval lands as BMS's existing myeloma franchise is being hollowed out by generics. Revlimid sales fell 49% year-over-year to $425 million in the second quarter of 2026; Pomalyst, hit by generic entry earlier this year, dropped 71% to $204 million[^3]. Zenbexus, priced at $29,500 per 28-day cycle, is one of the assets BMS is counting on to offset that decline. William Blair analysts project U.S. sales could top $1 billion annually by 2031[^4] — a number that assumes both a smooth rollout and no material erosion of the eligible patient pool in the meantime.

That second assumption is the one worth watching. Multiple myeloma has become a crowded field: CAR-T therapies Carvykti and Abecma, and bispecific antibodies including Tecvayli and Talvey, already compete for the same relapsed patients, and daratumumab-based regimens are increasingly used as early as first-line treatment — which, if the trend continues, could shrink the later-line population Zenbexus targets before it fully ramps[^4]. BMS shares rose roughly 1.5% on the approval day and have since traded in the mid-$60s, with Citi analysts framing the approval as a sign of the company's broader shift away from legacy-drug dependence[^4] — a reasonable read, though one that says more about portfolio narrative than about Zenbexus's standalone commercial ceiling.

The next checkpoint is less about the label and more about the label's durability: BMS's confirmatory trial data, and whether real-world uptake tracks the EXCALIBER-RRMM numbers once Zenbexus is competing for prescriptions rather than headlines.

uk-battery-fires-cost.headline: Battery fires at UK recycling centres now costing industry £1bn a year
uk-battery-fires-cost.body_md:
The economics of Britain's waste industry are being rewritten by something most households toss out without a second thought: the battery inside a broken vape, an old toothbrush, or a dead set of earbuds.

New estimates from the Environmental Services Association (ESA), the trade body for UK waste and recycling operators, put the cost of lithium-battery fires in the waste system at over £1 billion a year — up from roughly £150 million in 2021. The jump reflects not a single catastrophe but a steady accumulation of thousands of small ones: refuse trucks gutted mid-round, sorting lines shut down for days, insurance premiums climbing, and recycling centres rebuilt after blazes that often start with a single crushed cell.

![Batteries collected for recycling](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c0/Batteries_for_recycling.JPG)

## An epidemic, in the industry's own words

UK fire services tackled 1,760 lithium-ion battery fires in 2025 — one every five hours, and a 147% rise in three years, according to figures compiled by fire and waste bodies. More than 1,200 of those fires broke out specifically in bin lorries and waste facilities, a 71% jump on the year before. Roughly half of all waste fires are now attributed to lithium-ion cells.

"Waste fires caused by batteries not only endanger the lives of people working in essential frontline services but also destroy vital infrastructure," said Jacob Hayler, the ESA's executive director, in the trade body's most recent warning on the issue. The language — "epidemic levels" — is the ESA's own, and it is doing real work: it signals an industry group that has stopped treating this as an operational nuisance and started treating it as an existential cost problem it cannot absorb alone.

The mechanics are mundane and that is precisely the danger. A vape, a laptop battery or a cordless toothbrush thrown in with general rubbish gets compacted in a collection vehicle or shredded on a sorting line. If the cell is punctured or crushed, it can enter thermal runaway — a chemical reaction that ignites within seconds and is very hard to extinguish with water alone. Material Focus, the electricals-recycling body, estimates 1.6 billion batteries are discarded in household bins each year, more than a billion of them hidden inside everyday electricals rather than sold as standalone batteries.

## Who pays, and who doesn't

The striking feature of the £1bn figure is where it lands. Recycling and waste operators absorb the repair bills, the insurance hikes, the lost vehicles and the business interruption. The manufacturers whose products contain the batteries that start the fires do not currently bear any of that cost. That mismatch — cost falling on the handler of a battery's end-of-life, not the maker of its beginning-of-life — is the crux of what waste operators are now asking the government to fix.

London's four largest waste authorities wrote to the minister for nature, Mary Creagh, in November 2025 urging faster action. The ESA's own policy ask is more specific: mandatory kerbside collection of batteries and small electricals across England, funded through a reformed Extended Producer Responsibility scheme rather than left to supermarket bring-banks and household recycling centres. Independent analysis commissioned from the consultancy Eunomia suggests such a scheme, retrofitting collection vehicles with external battery containers at an estimated capital cost of around 70p per household, could save more than £6 billion over the next decade by cutting fires at source rather than fighting them after collection.

## What's next

A cross-party Lithium-ion Battery Safety Bill, introduced in the House of Lords in 2024, remains under debate and would tighten rules on the sale and disposal of battery-powered products, including a crackdown on non-compliant online sellers. Whether the government moves on the ESA's producer-funding ask — and how quickly — will determine whether the £1bn cost keeps rising or starts to fall. For battery and electronics manufacturers, the direction of travel is the same one now familiar from packaging and electricals EPR reform elsewhere: costs currently externalised onto waste operators are being eyed for redistribution back up the supply chain, with implications for anyone pricing battery-dependent products, EV components included, on the assumption that end-of-life costs stay someone else's problem.

uk-rail-el-nino-prep.headline: Britain's railways prepare for more extreme weather as intense El Niño develops
uk-rail-el-nino-prep.body_md:
Two trains derailed within 24 hours of each other on Britain's railways this month, during the fifth heatwave of the summer — an unremarkable-sounding statistic that Network Rail engineers describe as "exceptional." It is the kind of exceptional that forecasters now expect to become routine. The Met Office says an El Niño event now building in the Pacific is on track to be the strongest in more than a century, with sea-surface temperatures projected to peak more than 3°C above normal — well above the 1-2°C of a typical event.

"We're expecting the biggest El Niño for over a century," said Prof Adam Scaife, the Met Office's head of long-range forecasting. For the UK, the winter signature that follows is a familiar one: milder air and wetter, stormier weather. The Met Office's November-to-January outlook puts the probability of above-average temperatures at 55-65%, strongest in the south-east, and gives a 60% chance of an above-average storm season — ten or more named storms making landfall.

![Storm damage and sea-wall repairs at Dawlish, Devon, where a 2014 breach severed the only rail line into the South West for eight weeks](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7a/South_Devon_Railway_sea_wall_breach_February_2014.JPG)

## A budget line that keeps growing

For Network Rail, the state-owned infrastructure manager, weather resilience has quietly become one of the fastest-growing items in its capital programme rather than an occasional emergency cost. In its current five-year funding round, Control Period 7, running to 2029, the company is directing roughly £2.8bn toward drainage and earthworks — reinforcing more than 480km of embankments and cuttings, laying over 600,000 metres of new drainage, and recruiting some 400 specialist engineers. That figure represents roughly five times the equivalent allocation set five years earlier, a jump that followed a taskforce review, led by geotechnical engineer Lord Robert Mair, commissioned after the fatal Stonehaven derailment in 2020.

The scale of that reallocation illustrates the underlying problem: infrastructure sized for one climate is being asked to perform in another. Britain's railway was engineered for a temperature band of roughly -10°C to 20°C, said Xueyu Geng, professor of ground engineering at the University of Warwick — a tolerance dwarfed by systems in Spain (0°C to 45°C) or Saudi Arabia (10°C to 55°C), where infrastructure was designed with far wider swings in mind from the outset. "I believe Network Rail has done a great job to maintain our railway network, but we still need to be able to adapt more in order to cope with this changing climate," Geng said.

The cautionary precedent is Dawlish. When a storm surge breached the sea wall at the Devon coastal town in February 2014, tearing away 80 metres of track, it took eight weeks and roughly £35m to reopen the line — the only rail connection into the South West — with the closure estimated to have cost the regional economy up to £1.2bn. Network Rail has since spent £165m reinforcing that stretch of coastline alone, a single-location bill that underscores how expensive reactive repair is next to planned adaptation.

That arithmetic is now the operative question for this winter: whether drainage clearance, culvert inspections and earthwork monitoring, the maintenance measures Network Rail is racing to complete before the wetter season arrives, prove cheaper than another storm-forced closure. The answer will show up first in delay-minute data and infrastructure-fault reports once the named storms start arriving, and later in whether Network Rail's regulator, the Office of Rail and Road, judges the current funding settlement adequate when Control Period 8 planning begins.
