european-heatwave-death-toll.headline: European heatwave death toll passes 25,000 as wildfires burn 250,000 hectares
european-heatwave-death-toll.body_md:
Europe is closing out its deadliest summer in over a decade, and the final number is still moving. Heat-linked deaths across the continent passed 25,000 in early August, according to Bloomberg's tally of national mortality data — and by this week, Europe's excess-mortality monitoring hub was already reporting more than 30,000. The gap between those two figures, three weeks apart, is itself the story: official heat-death counts are structurally built to lag the events that cause them, and this summer has stretched that lag further than usual.

Alongside the deaths, more than 500,000 hectares have burned across the European Union by the most recent count from the EU's fire information system — well above the 20-year average of under 200,000 hectares for the same point in the season, and running ahead of even last year's record pace. France and Spain have each endured the largest single wildfires in their modern history. Both countries have carried out mass evacuations, and one crisis — a European river running dry — has quietly connected the heat deaths, the fires and a very different casualty: the continent's cruise and energy infrastructure.

## Counting the dead, weeks behind

Heat mortality is never announced in real time. It is reconstructed afterward, by comparing actual deaths against a statistical baseline of what would normally be expected — a method that requires weeks of national registry data to settle. EuroMOMO, the pooled European monitoring platform, put excess deaths at 14,260 for a single week in late June alone, with more than 12,000 of those among people over 65. Belgium's excess-mortality rate hit 48% that week, ahead of France at 23% and the Netherlands at 13%. Germany's Robert Koch Institute has separately estimated close to 12,000 heat-linked excess deaths since April, the highest national toll on the continent.

By the time Bloomberg's compiled figure crossed 25,000 in early August, the underlying week-by-week data it drew on was already a month old. That is the pattern epidemiologists flag every heatwave season: the headline number is real, but it is a floor, not a ceiling. This week's 30,000-plus reading from EuroMOMO suggests the eventual, fully reconciled total — the kind of number that arrives only after autumn, once every national registry has caught up — will land meaningfully higher again. Whether 2026 ultimately exceeds 2022's estimated 61,600 European heat deaths, still the modern benchmark, is a question the data cannot yet answer.

## Fire follows the heat

The wildfires are the visible half of the same event. In France, a blaze near Bordeaux burned through the Gironde and Landes, growing large enough to generate its own lightning and weather — a pyrocumulonimbus event never previously recorded in the country, and one more commonly associated with fire behaviour in North America or Australia. It forced evacuations that peaked above 250,000 people in France alone, with the Cap Ferret peninsula cleared entirely by boat and road. France has now burned more than 115,000 hectares this year, a national record.

![A water-bombing helicopter drops on a forest fire between Nantua and Les Neyrolles, France, July 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0c/H%C3%A9licopt%C3%A8re_bombardier_d%27eau%2C_feu_de_for%C3%AAt%2C_Nantua_et_Les_Neyrolles%2C_8_juillet_2026_en_fin_de_journ%C3%A9e_%283%29.jpg)

Spain declared a national emergency after a fire in Ávila province, west of Madrid, burned roughly 50,000 hectares — described by officials as the largest in the country's recorded history. Madrid deployed nearly 2,700 personnel, plus reinforcements from Greece, Italy and Portugal, a reminder that Europe's firefighting capacity is now routinely pooled across borders rather than handled nationally.

![Aid workers respond to wildfires in Ávila province, Spain, July 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b0/WCK_Responds_to_Wildfires_in_%C3%81vila_Province%2C_Spain_-_55419151327.jpg)

## When infrastructure meets its limit

The same heat that fed the fires has been drying out Europe's rivers, and that has turned into an economic story of its own. The Danube fell toward record-low levels in August, exposing sandbanks and shipwrecks from Belgrade to Budapest. In Hungary, the Paks nuclear plant — which depends on river water for cooling — was forced to run at roughly a tenth of its normal capacity, tightening the country's power supply during the same weeks that air-conditioning demand was peaking.

![Satellite comparison of the Danube's water levels near Budapest, August 2025 versus August 2026](https://www.esa.int/var/esa/storage/images/esa_multimedia/images/2026/08/danube_s_waters_fall_to_record_lows/27408537-1-eng-GB/Danube_s_waters_fall_to_record_lows.jpg)

On the same stretch of river, TUI's river cruises ran into a smaller but telling version of the same problem. Passengers on Danube sailings described broken air conditioning, sewage smells and non-functioning toilets through the peak of the heat — one traveller reported "big blowers" installed in place of proper cooling, pushing hot air through cabins already at 40°C outside. TUI has acknowledged that low water levels compounded the strain on its onboard systems and says it will invest in fleet-wide air conditioning upgrades this winter. It is a small case study in a larger question the summer has posed to industries well beyond travel: infrastructure built for the climate of a decade ago is now routinely tested by conditions it wasn't designed to survive.

## What comes next

The reconciled, final mortality figures for this summer won't be settled until national statistics offices close out autumn registry data — the point at which 2022's 61,600 figure was itself confirmed, months after the season ended. Insurers are watching the same lag from the other direction: wildfire and business-interruption claims from France and Spain are still being filed, and reinsurers will use this season, alongside 2022's, to judge whether 25,000-plus heat deaths and half a million hectares burned is becoming Europe's new one-in-ten-year event rather than an outlier. The next firm marker is EuroMOMO's autumn reconciliation, expected to either confirm or push past this week's 30,000-plus reading.

man-utd-baleba-transfer.headline: Man Utd agree £70m fee for Brighton's Baleba
man-utd-baleba-transfer.body_md:
Manchester United have agreed a deal worth up to £70m to sign Carlos Baleba from Brighton, one of the largest fees paid by an English club this summer and a reminder that Premier League spending shows no sign of slowing even as clubs across the division tighten belts elsewhere.

The structure is straightforward by the standards of a market that increasingly hides its true price in add-ons: £65m guaranteed, another £5m in performance-related payments, and a sell-on clause that gives Brighton a cut of any future sale. The 22-year-old Cameroon international will sign a five-year contract once his medical is complete, though he will not play for some weeks — Baleba is recovering from an ankle ligament injury picked up in pre-season and is not expected to be fit until around mid-September.

![Carlos Baleba in action for Brighton](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/09/Carlos_Baleba_2026.jpg)

## Brighton's conveyor belt

The deal is also the latest instalment in one of English football's more reliable success stories: Brighton's ability to keep selling its best players without appearing to weaken. Baleba himself arrived at the Amex in 2023 for around £23m, signed from Lille as the direct replacement for Moises Caicedo — who left for Chelsea that same year for a then British-record £115m. When Brighton lost Yves Bissouma to Tottenham, they had Caicedo ready. When they lost Caicedo, they had Baleba. The pattern has held long enough that it no longer looks like luck.

For Manchester United, Baleba becomes the third midfielder recruited this summer, following the arrivals of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans. Sky Sports's football desk framed the appeal in blunt terms: he offers "specialist defensive power coupled with the athleticism to drive United up the pitch" — the kind of ball-winning profile United have chased, with mixed results, since Paul Pogba's departure. It is worth noting his stock has cooled slightly: a year ago Brighton were said to want more than £100m for him, above Caicedo's fee, before a dip in form during the 2025-26 season brought the price back to earth.

## A market that won't cool down

What makes the fee notable beyond United's own rebuild is the context around it. Premier League clubs had already spent roughly £2.14bn this summer with two weeks of the window still to run, putting the division on course to beat — or at least match — last year's record outlay of around £3.1bn. Chelsea lead the individual spending charts, with net outlay estimated between £183m and £242m; Arsenal, Manchester City and promoted Ipswich also feature prominently.

That spending is happening just as the Premier League's financial framework is being rewritten. The current Profit and Sustainability Rules, which cap cumulative losses at £105m over three years, are being replaced from next season by a Squad Cost Ratio system that ties permitted spending on wages, agent fees and transfer amortisation to a fixed share — 85% — of club revenue. The shift explains some of the urgency: clubs have an incentive to complete big-ticket deals under the old regime before the new ratio bites, and to structure fees like Baleba's — modest guaranteed sum, meaningful add-ons, a sell-on clause protecting the selling club — in ways that spread cost and risk under either rulebook.

Brighton, for their part, keep proving that selling well is its own competitive advantage. The next name to watch from the production line is Kaoru Mitoma, whom Al Nassr have already tried and failed to prise away once. Baleba is expected to make his United debut only after the derby with Manchester City on 13 September and the visit of Fulham a week later — by which point the picture of who actually won this transfer window will be considerably clearer.

arsenal-open-title-defence.headline: Arsenal open title defence with comfortable win over Coventry
arsenal-open-title-defence.body_md:
Arsenal's title defence began the way pre-season suggested it would: comfortably. A 3-0 win over newly promoted Coventry City at the Emirates on Friday evening gave Mikel Arteta's side the perfect start to the 2026-27 Premier League season, five days after the same scoreline was inflicted on Manchester City in the Community Shield.

![Emirates Stadium, Arsenal's home ground](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a3/Emirates_Stadium_Arsenal.jpg)

Kai Havertz opened the scoring in the 15th minute, converting a Riccardo Calafiori cross, before Bukayo Saka doubled the lead eight minutes later after Coventry's defence got tangled up dealing with Christos Tzolis. Captain Martin Ødegaard added a third shortly after the interval, and from there the afternoon settled into the kind of one-way procession the champions have made routine at home.

## A statement, not a surprise

Arsenal ended a 22-year wait for the title last season, and the calculus around them this year is less "can they win it" than "who stops them." Manchester City are mid-transition, Liverpool are still rebuilding after finishing fifth, and bookmakers had already installed Arsenal as favourites — priced around 11/10 — before a ball was kicked. Two routine wins over the league's two most recent champions in the space of five days does nothing to disturb that consensus.

> "There was a lot to like. Obviously it was a great result, but the manner we started the game — the domination, clarity, understanding and growth in the game — was really impressive," Arteta said afterwards.

He was measured on the opponent, too: "They are a really good side, really well-coached and clear in the way they want to hurt you. We didn't give them chances until the last minutes." The win was also a personal landmark — Arteta's 150th Premier League victory in charge, reached in fewer games than all but four managers in the competition's history.

## Coventry's reality check

For Coventry, back in the top flight for the first time since relegation in 2001, the lesson was the blunter one. Frank Lampard's side won the Championship by 11 points last season and arrived at the Emirates with a reputation for organisation and control in possession. None of it travelled. Coventry barely troubled David Raya's goal and looked overrun for long stretches against a squad several levels deeper in quality — the gap between the Championship's best and the Premier League's champions, laid bare in real time.

It is one match, and newly promoted sides have escaped worse afternoons to survive comfortably; Coventry's season will be judged over 38 games, not one. But as an opening data point, it confirms what most expected: this is a heavy year of adjustment ahead for a club that hasn't sat at English football's top table for a quarter of a century.

The result changes nothing beyond the three points. Arsenal's title odds were already short; Coventry's survival odds were already long. Both now have a Premier League table to build a season around, starting with Arsenal's trip to face one of last season's top-six sides next and Coventry's first home top-flight fixture in 25 years.

mps-hospitality-disclosures.headline: MPs accused of 'failing to learn' after accepting £400,000 in hospitality
mps-hospitality-disclosures.body_md:
There is a familiar rhythm to these disclosures now. A concert, a cup final, an awards ceremony — an MP's name against a four-figure sum, filed quietly in the Register of Members' Financial Interests, then gathered up months later into a headline figure large enough to make people wince. This time the number is just under £400,000, the freebies span January to July 2026, and the reaction from transparency campaigners is closer to weary than shocked.

> "Some ministers and MPs appear to have short memories of the freebie-gate scandal that engulfed the first few months of Starmer's time in No 10," said Sue Hawley, director of Spotlight on Corruption.

**In one sentence:** MPs across parties declared close to £400,000 in tickets and hospitality this year, reviving the freebies row that dogged the start of Keir Starmer's premiership.

![Palace of Westminster, seen from across the Thames](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/Palace_of_Westminster%2C_Houses_of_Parliament%2C_London%2C_UK.jpg)

## The list

The entries read like a summer social calendar rather than a scandal ledger. Education Secretary Lucy Powell took £858 tickets to see Harry Styles at Wembley, courtesy of the music industry body PRS. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Attorney General Ellie Reeves each declared hospitality worth over £1,300 — the Chelsea Flower Show for Streeting, courtesy of Lloyds Banking Group, and the Ivor Novello Awards for Reeves, alongside Louise Haigh. Chief Whip Anneliese Midgley notched up roughly £4,300 across the Brit Awards, Cheltenham Festival and the Grand National. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander watched the Wimbledon men's final courtesy of a £1,480 hospitality package, and Andy Burnham's declarations for the year run to around £6,000, including a £3,800 Brit Awards appearance in Manchester.

The Conservatives are not spared the comparison. Leader Kemi Badenoch accepted £1,360 of Wimbledon hospitality from the All England Club, while shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow business secretary Andrew Griffith took Chelsea Flower Show and Formula One tickets worth similar sums. None of it, on the record so far, breaches parliamentary rules — hospitality above £300 simply has to be declared within 28 days, and by that narrow measure the system worked exactly as designed.

## Why the déjà vu

That is precisely the campaigners' complaint. Rules that require disclosure rather than restraint tend to produce disclosure rather than restraint — and Westminster has been here before. Starmer's own early months in office were consumed by the row over free clothing and football tickets from Labour donor Waheed Alli, a controversy serious enough that the prime minister eventually stopped accepting personal gifts of clothing altogether. The expectation, inside and outside Parliament, was that the episode would chasten members across the House. The 2026 numbers suggest it mostly chastened them into finding new categories of freebie.

Duncan Hames of Transparency International UK put the underlying tension plainly: "Just because something is permitted it is not necessarily appropriate." It is a distinction the current disclosure regime is not built to enforce. The Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards can investigate breaches of the rules, but accepting a declared, permitted gift is not a breach — it is compliance. Critics argue that is exactly the problem: a threshold-and-declare system polices paperwork, not judgment, and judgment is what kept failing.

## What's next

No new sanctions or rule changes have followed the disclosures, and none appear imminent — the Committee on Standards has not signalled a fresh review. The more likely test comes the next time a high-value gift lands close to an unrelated vote or contract decision, at which point "permitted" and "appropriate" will be forced apart in public rather than in a campaigner's quote. Until then, the register will keep filling up, and the retrospective tallies will keep landing every few months, each one bigger than campaigners would like and each one, technically, within the rules.

england-first-test-takeaways.headline: England's first Test takeaways as 'Fab Four' era faces new challengers
england-first-test-takeaways.body_md:
England did not so much win the first Test against Pakistan as demolish it. An innings and 103 runs, wrapped up before tea on day three at Headingley, is the kind of scoreline that flatters nobody's uncertainty — and after a torrid few months for English cricket, uncertainty was exactly what hung over this match before a ball was bowled.

The game arrived as the first assignment of a rebuilt England: Joe Root back in the captaincy eight weeks after Ben Stokes's shock retirement from international cricket mid-way through a losing series against New Zealand, Brendon McCullum gone from the red-ball coaching post, and Kiwi veteran Stephen Fleming installed alongside him. If that sounds like a lot of change to absorb before Pakistan even turned up, it was. Root's response was to skittle the tourists for 171, pile up 409 in reply, and bowl them out again for 135 — the kind of statement that buys a new regime some breathing room.

![Joe Root, restored as England's Test captain, in national colours](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/England_captain_Joe_Root_2019.jpg)

## A captaincy return built on substance, not nostalgia

Root led England 64 times between 2017 and 2022 with a reputation, fairly or not, for over-thinking the job. This time the tone was different. Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue took five-wicket hauls in the same innings — the first England pace pair to do it against Pakistan since 1998 — with Robinson removing the ninth wicket and Tongue the tenth on consecutive deliveries, a first in Test history. Root left out a frontline spinner at Headingley, backed four seamers instead, and it worked before lunch on day one.

"Judge me not on how I was last time, but how I am now," Root told Michael Atherton afterwards. "It was never trying to be Ben Stokes. It was just Joe Root being Joe." Former England captain Nasser Hussain, watching from the commentary box, called it composure across "decision-making, batting and field management" — a pointed contrast with a player who, by his own admission, used to find the captaincy a weight rather than a tool.

The personal milestones piled up alongside the team performance. Root's fielding effort to remove Pakistan opener Azan Awais took him to 219 Test catches, moving him past Steve Smith's 218 to become the outright leading catcher, wicketkeepers included, in the format's history. He also became the first captain to pass 3,000 runs in the World Test Championship era. At 35 and 166 Tests into a career now closing in on Sachin Tendulkar's all-time run tally, Root remains the last man standing from cricket's celebrated "Fab Four."

## The Fab Four's long goodbye

That quartet — Root, Virat Kohli, Steve Smith and Kane Williamson — was coined by Martin Crowe more than a decade ago to describe the batters who would define an era. The era, on current evidence, is ending in instalments. Kohli has retired from Tests and T20Is. Williamson has stepped away from international cricket entirely. Smith no longer plays ODIs and, at 37, is into the twilight of his Test career. Root, still scoring and now captaining again, is the exception rather than the rule — which is precisely why his second stint carries more scrutiny than his first. He is no longer simply England's best batter; he is the last of a generation still auditioning as its own successor.

![Harry Brook, England's vice-captain, batting for Yorkshire](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/60/Harry_Brook_%2851225504151%29.jpg)

The candidates to inherit the mantle are increasingly named in the same breath: India's Shubman Gill and Yashasvi Jaiswal, New Zealand's Rachin Ravindra, and England's own Harry Brook, who made 91 at Headingley and was dismissed — like three other England batters — by Pakistan debutant left-armer Ali Usman, who claimed five wickets on his first day in Test cricket. Kane Williamson himself has floated Brook's name as a natural heir. Root, for his part, has called Brook "far and away the best batter in the world" on current form. Jordan Cox, uncapped before this year, made 73 in a 150-run stand with his captain and looks like the next name England will build an order around.

## What Headingley actually proved, and what it didn't

The caveat, and it is a significant one, is Pakistan. A touring side that has been in near-permanent turmoil off the field found four of its top six dismissed for single figures across the two innings, and only Mohammad Rizwan (41) and opener Shafique (61 in the first innings) offered sustained resistance. An innings win over an out-of-sorts Pakistan attack tells England less about its depth than a contest with India or Australia would. The batting collapse that undid the previous regime against New Zealand two months ago has not been retested here.

What Headingley does confirm is personnel: Cox and Emilio Gay pushing for permanent middle-order and opening slots, Brook established as vice-captain and lead run-scorer in waiting, and a four-man pace attack — Robinson, Tongue, Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson — that looks capable of bowling out most sides twice inside three days on a helpful surface. Whether that holds on flatter pitches, against sharper batting orders, is the question this series was designed to start answering, not finish.

The second Test begins Thursday at Lord's, with Pakistan hoping to have captain Babar Azam back from a finger injury — a return that would test England's bowling attack against opposition rather better equipped to survive it. That, more than anything at Headingley, will show whether this is a genuine changing of the guard or simply one bad Pakistan performance flattering a team still finding its post-Stokes shape.

burnham-whitehall-officials.headline: Burnham to dispatch 100 Whitehall officials to bolster regional mayors' offices
burnham-whitehall-officials.body_md:
There is a particular irony in Andy Burnham running Whitehall now. For a decade he was the mayor who needled London for hoarding power over Manchester's buses, its housing, its growth funding. On Friday, a month into his premiership, he sat in his northern outpost and announced that Whitehall would start sending its people north — not the other way round.

The plan: more than 100 civil servants seconded from central government departments into the offices of regional mayors, five to 10 apiece, across a pilot covering 18 mayoralties from the autumn. Secondments run six to nine months, and mayors get to request the skills they need — a planner here, a finance specialist there. The government has billed it as the "largest transfer of Whitehall capacity to local leaders yet."

> "The days of Westminster hoarding power are over." — Louise Haigh, First Secretary of State

![Andy Burnham, now Prime Minister, pictured in an official portrait taken at 10 Downing Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Haigh's framing — Whitehall giving up ground rather than reasserting it — is the government's line, and it fits the broader project. Burnham has already relocated a slice of the Prime Minister's operation itself to Manchester, branding it No10 North, working out of Heron House while a permanent campus is built on Great Ancoats Street. He calls it "the nerve centre of a rewired Britain." Chancellor John Healey has called growth a "dual mission between No 11 and No 10 North."

## Whose officials are they, really

The secondment model cuts the other way too. The 100 officials being placed inside mayoral offices remain Whitehall employees, on loans of under a year, reporting up a Whitehall chain even as they sit at a mayor's table. Critics inside and outside the civil service reform world have been blunt about what that tends to produce. Writing in City AM, one commentator argued that since devolution began in 2014, Whitehall's own headcount has grown by almost 120,000 — the pattern being that the centre doesn't shrink when it hands out responsibility, it "metamorphoses into a regulatory state," trading direct control for outcomes frameworks, program boards and reporting lines that still run through London.

IPPR North's Mirte Boot put the more sympathetic version of the same doubt more gently: the plan "establishes the plumbing, but the water isn't flowing yet" — meaning the money hasn't moved, only the staff have. That matters because roughly 95% of UK tax revenue still flows to the Treasury, the highest centralisation ratio in the G7. Scotland's John Swinney dismissed the announcement as rhetoric without fiscal substance; Wales's Rhun ap Iorwerth warned it risked becoming "Whitehall with a different postcode."

Burnham's team says the real test comes in October, when the Budget is expected to set out how much local income tax revenue mayors get to keep and control — the piece of devolution that would actually change who decides how the money is spent, rather than who sits in the room while it's decided. Until then, 100 secondees moving north look less like a transfer of power than a transfer of personnel, with the ledger still kept in London.

ns-i-premium-bonds-rate.headline: NS&I raises Premium Bonds prize fund rate again, improving odds of a win
ns-i-premium-bonds-rate.body_md:
Premium Bonds have never paid a fixed return — that has always been the point, and the source of a certain low-grade national anxiety every time the prize draw lands and the text message doesn't come. But the odds of getting anything at all just got a little better, for the second time this year.

National Savings & Investments said the prize fund rate will rise to 4.35% from the September draw, up from 3.8% in July and 3.3% in April. The chance of any single £1 bond winning something shortens to 1 in 21,000, from 1 in 22,000. It sounds like a modest tweak. In practice it means NS&I is adding roughly £63 million to the monthly prize pot and creating more than 308,000 extra prizes compared with August — everything from an additional dozen jackpots at £100,000 down to thousands more £25 payouts.

![A money box modelled on ERNIE, the machine that has picked Premium Bonds winners since 1957](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/Money_box_shaped_like_ERNIE_the_Computer_%28Science_Museum%2C_London%29.jpg)

## Why NS&I keeps moving the dial

Premium Bonds are, formally, a Treasury-backed savings product with no interest at all — savers forgo a guaranteed return in exchange for a shot at tax-free prizes, picked monthly by ERNIE, the Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment that has done the job in various incarnations since 1957. What has changed is not the mechanism but the incentive behind it. NS&I operates under an annual net financing target set by the Treasury — currently £15 billion, give or take £4 billion — meaning it needs to pull in (or hold onto) a specific volume of retail deposits each year. When commercial banks and challenger apps are paying more to attract savers, NS&I has to sweeten Premium Bonds or watch the money walk.

That competitive pressure has been intense. Some easy-access accounts are advertising rates as high as 5% including introductory bonuses, and top cash ISAs are paying up to 4.56%, tax-free and guaranteed — no dice roll required. April's rate cut to 3.3% now looks, in hindsight, like NS&I misjudging how sticky that competition would be; the reversal back up to 4.35% in five months suggests the correction was more urgent than a routine review.

## The gap between headline and lived experience

The prize fund rate is a statistical average across the roughly £132 billion held in Premium Bonds by more than 22 million holders, not a promise to any individual saver. Someone holding the maximum £50,000 will, over enough draws, land close to the advertised rate. Someone holding a few hundred pounds may well go years without winning a penny, luck being what it is. That asymmetry is precisely why financial advisers tend to steer smaller savers toward an ISA or a fixed-rate bond, where the return is contractual rather than probabilistic — and it is why, even at 4.35%, Premium Bonds remain a product bought as much for the tax-free lottery thrill and capital security as for expected value.

## What it says about the wider savings market

None of this moves markets. But it is a useful barometer: even a government-backed product with no obligation to compete on headline rates is being forced to, twice in five months, because deposit competition among banks and NS&I's own financing needs leave it no room not to. The next test comes whenever the Bank of England next adjusts its base rate — a cut would ease the pressure on commercial banks' savings rates and could, in time, give NS&I room to ease off the accelerator again.
